utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would the registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case IT-05-87-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Milutinovic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, I'm Tom Hannis. I'm joined today by Mr. Chester Stamp, who is my co-counsel in this case, and on my left is Susan Grogan, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Eugene O'Sullivan appearing on behalf of Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I'm Toma Fila. I'm appearing for Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I'm Milan Petrovic, and I'm appearing on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Tomislav Visnjic appearing on behalf of General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman appearing on behalf of General Pavkovic, and with me is Aleksandar Aleksic also appearing as co-counsel in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, I'm Mihajlo Bakrac appearing on behalf of General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCUDDER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'm Theodore Scudder appearing on behalf of Sreten Lukic, and I'm assisted here by Mr. Dragan Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this afternoon is a Status Conference. I won't try to give it an identification number because it probably is a different one for almost each of the accused here. We have now for the first time a total of six accused represented at this one Status Conference. There are two accused present. They are Mr. Petrovic and Mr. Lukic. I address them for the moment just to confirm that they are able to understand these proceedings in a language that's familiar to them. Is that the position for you, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Pavkovic. My mistake, sorry. Mr. Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can follow the proceedings in language that I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I'm going to deal with quite a number of matters this afternoon, and I want to deal first of all with outstanding motions or issues which require determination either here or by the Trial Chamber. And the first of these is a Prosecution motion for protective measures which relates to two particular witnesses designed to give evidence about intercepted communications. There is a matter for the Trial Chamber to determine possibly in relation to this motion. One of the problems related to it is that the motion contains a number of measures which it sought to introduce in the course of these witnesses' evidence, and because these are measures insisted upon by the state from which these witnesses come, the Trial Chamber is probably in the position of either accepting these measures and allowing evidence in that way or in the way sought or refusing to hear the witnesses, which may be an unfortunate position for the Trial Chamber, because it may have sympathy with some of the measures sought and may feel that others go too far. Now, I gather the matter was raised at the 65 ter Conference, and what I'd like to know from Mr. Hannis is whether he is any further forward in identifying whether all of these measures are actually insisted upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to say I don't have that information for you yet, but I do now have the name of the appropriate person to discuss those matters with, and I will be doing that shortly and advising you through your legal officer as soon as I have that information, and I will advise him of the concerns that have been expressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For example, the Chamber might well be sympathetic to the part of the motion which would restrict or prevent cross-examination about the means by which these communications were intercepted. In other words, issues that might relate to national security. On the other hand, the Chamber might not be too sympathetic to restricting cross-examination on a broader basis than that in a preliminary decision. Any further restriction might be best dealt with in the course of the trial by objection to particular questions or lines of questioning that are taken up. So there's a distinction there in relation to the two separate requests to restrict cross-examination. There's also a question over whether it's necessary for a representative of the state to be present. Now, if there is no agreement on exactly how cross-examination is to be limited, then there may be a good argument for a representative of the state to be present. If, on the other hand, agreement can be reached then it would appear to be unnecessary. And likewise, I think I indicated at the last Status Conference for the first three accused here that I was hopeful that counsel might get closer to the stage of being able to stipulate at least some of the elements that arise from this particular evidence. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan, can you tell me if there's any progress on that front or whether progress is impossible because of the lack of information from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The position hasn't changed in any substance since we met in May. I don't think it's impossible that we advance on this, but there has been no movement at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the motion in this case is made in the original case of Milutinovic and two co-accused, but presumably, Mr. Hannis, you want the same arrangements to apply in relation to all six accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And I assume that when I speak with the appropriate Croatian authorities I will bring that to their attention. I anticipate that this will involve six accused, and I assume they would be requesting the same things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be that the evidence doesn't affect three of the accused directly. It may effect them indirectly because of the issue of joint criminal enterprise but it may not affect them directly. But it raises the technical question of whether in fact you ought to submit another motion, which is a motion in the case involving all six accused rather than a motion that's confined to three.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That -- I take your point, Your Honour. That may be a good course of action, and I can do that once I've spoken with them and maybe reached some agreement about diminishing or removing some of the current requested measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be at the same time you ought to review all the motions in this case that have actually -- in both cases of that been determined so far to decide whether you actually need to lodge some composite motion to give effect to these in the conjoined case, but I -- it's a matter I understand from the 65 ter Conference you at least have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We do now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So do you think the appropriate course in relation to the current motion is for the Trial Chamber to take no further action until it hears further from you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that's -- unless any counsel for the accused has any other comment to make on that, that's the course of action I would propose to take. The second outstanding motion is Mr. Lukic's emergency motion for provisional release which has now become not an emergency motion but has really been converted into a broader motion for provisional release. All filings have now been received by the Chamber in relation to that and a decision will be made by the Chamber as soon as possible. Now, I don't think, Mr. Scudder, that anything else needs to be done in relation to that today. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCUDDER
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. The third one is the second request, or the amended request, rather, to NATO and the states of NATO at the incidence of General Ojdanic under Rule 54 bis. Now, there are certain ongoing discussions, as I understand it. These affect certain of the states. It may not effect them all. And the indication I was given following the 65 ter Conference was at least in relation to the states with whom discussions are ongoing and perhaps in relation to others that it would be premature to make a final decision on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this application at the moment. Now, Mr. Visnjic, what is the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I would like to say that I owe you an explanation from the 65 ter Conference that concerns part of the request with regard to Holland. Before we applied for the send time, the Dutch government responded in satisfactory way, and that's why it is not listed as one of the states from which we have requested documents in our second application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you will not be proceeding against the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They have met our requests, and that is why they have not been listed in our second application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I understand that there are ongoing discussions with at least two states. Does that mean that it's premature to make any final decision in relation to any of the states at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that a partial decision with regard to other states would be premature. I believe that they would all have to be encompassed with one decision. Even the ongoing correspondence that we have with two states according to the current situation will lead to the partial satisfaction of our request, but we have to take our position with regard to the final set of documents that we received from them, and we will inform the Chamber accordingly. It would be more rational in my view if a decision -- one decision was rendered for all the states instead of rendering two separate decisions. We will have the final outcome of our correspondence very soon, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the matter will remain with you to notify the Trial Chamber with a further filing when it's appropriate for a decision to be taken, and can I take it that in that filing you will indicate anything that you want to modify or vary or withdraw in relation to the application?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the fourth motion is that at the instance of General Pavkovic for disclosure. Now, Mr. Ackerman, there seems to be a measure of confusion about how this should be dealt with. What is sought is access to material in the case of Slobodan Milosevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I'm asking for is all of the trial transcripts and exhibits from the Milosevic trial as it respects Kosovo and make that an ongoing request because the trial is still going on, including all of the -- all of the protected material, the closed session and private sessions and the whole thing. I filed it in the wrong case, I understand, and although it's the same Judges, what I will do is just change the heading on it and refile it probably as early as Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I -- that may be just jumping the gun a little. The -- have you looked at all at what arrangements have been made for disclosure from the Milosevic case in relation to your now co-accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I learned, I think maybe from the agenda for the 65 ter Conference, that there was an outstanding order of some form regarding disclosure of Milosevic matters, but I don't know the extent of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there is an order, and it's even given rise to concern that perhaps it hasn't been implemented as well as it ought to be. I think maybe Mr. O'Sullivan has raised that issue in relation to his client.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He spoke about that at the 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the order is there, and it's simply an order on counsel to liaise with the Registrar. It's an order reminding the Prosecution of its obligation, and it makes it clear that counsel can apply to the Trial Chamber where satisfactory arrangements for disclosure are not made. Now, I don't think at this stage it's necessary for the Trial Chamber in the Milosevic case to be involved in this. I mean, have you asked the Prosecution for the material?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've spoken to the Registry about it, and they said they would give it to me as soon as an appropriate order was entered by the Chamber, and that's as far as I've gone. I take it from what Your Honour is telling me now the order -- the order from the -- the order applies to the new three defendants even though it's not couched that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I'm surprised that the Registry took that view in light of the terms of the existing order. It does only apply in the original case, which is the case against the first three accused, but I find it difficult to see why there should be a need for any other order when the terms of that order were simply for the accused to liaise with the registrar to establish mutually convenient methods of provision of the transcripts of all open-session proceedings and all public exhibits, and the Prosecution were reminded of an obligation to ensure that closed-session transcripts were reviewed and submitted for release on an ongoing basis and in a timely fashion. So I don't see the need for an order from the Trial Chamber for this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It sounds, Your Honour, that the matter might have been taken in hand before and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Someone from the Registry did tell you that you would require an order?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that was in the context of my advising the Registry that I'd filed a motion and that I thought it may be appropriate to wait until that motion had been granted with regard to the -- to the non-public materials so that everything could be provided to me in a -- in an orderly manner rather than piecemeal. So that was the basis of the Registry's position, that they would await the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Somewhat to my suggestion that they do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm reminded that the original order, in fact, only applied to the second and third accused and didn't actually apply to Mr. Milutinovic, and yet it has been implemented, as I understand it, in relation to Mr. Milutinovic. Is that right, Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Excuse me. I have been receiving the transcript and exhibits. The only concern or perhaps portion that needs to be covered are any confidential exhibits, if any, or exhibits from closed session, not just the public exhibits, which are relevant to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thanks. Mr. Hannis, this can, I think, be resolved by you quite simply. I take it that there is absolutely no difficulty about the Prosecution ensuring that closed-session transcripts and indeed exhibits which are not -- or which are in any way under seal or restricted are released on an ongoing basis to all -- those acting for all six accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understood this was a responsibility for the Registry rather than for our office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's not the position in this order. The order, so far as closed-session material is concerned, and I think by analogy I would apply it to exhibits as well that were restricted in any way is that -- the terms of the order were to remind the Prosecution of its obligation to ensure that that material was disclosed, and I suspect that's because you're best placed to make sure that nothing that shouldn't escape your clutches or the clutches of the records is passed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But in any event, I take it that assuming we identify who has been doing this that you accept that it should apply to all six accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I take it you also accept that it should apply not only to transcripts of oral evidence but should apply to documentary evidence as well and any exhibits involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So it seems to me that it's a matter for Defence counsel to arrange with the Registrar. I will make sure -- and to liaise with Mr. Hannis to make sure that whatever the Registrar is not providing he provides to you, and I will ensure that a transcript of this exchange is passed to the Registry so that you can complete your discussions with them. And in the light of that, what I would prefer you to do today, Mr. Ackerman, is withdraw your motion. Obviously if anything -- if things don't work out the way we've discussed, you would be able to re-enroll, retender the motion but in the right process.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll do that. I do now withdraw the motion. But let me mention to you an additional problem that Mr. O'Sullivan raised in the 65 ter, and that is the Registry's response, as I understand it, has been that the transcripts are available on the Internet and all we have to do is go to the Milosevic part of the Internet and download them. And the problem is those are not transcripts that have the appropriate headings on them like the official transcripts that -- that we would get similar to what we got from yesterday's conference, for instance, and we need the official transcripts so we can have the headings that would make it possible for us to make some sense of them. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I understand from the senior legal officer that the matter was taken up with the Registrar yesterday following the 65 ter Conference and has been resolved so far as the first accused is concerned, and I can see no reason why it shouldn't be resolved in relation to everyone in the same way. So, again, I simply request that you liaise with the Registry to solve this problem and to raise it with the Trial Chamber only if you cannot do so by your own efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There is one final dimension to receiving materials from the Milosevic proceedings, and that is exhibits which are marked for identification purposes only but which have not been admitted into evidence. I don't care where they come from, whether it comes from the Registry or Prosecutor, but to make any sense of understanding the testimony of a witness we need to also have exhibits which have only been marked for identification and not yet admitted into evidence, otherwise we can read pages of transcript where questioning is going on in relation to a document, for example, which we may not receive if we only receive the exhibits, and it is relevant to our case preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that comment confined to Prosecution exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, it's not. All exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, there doesn't seem to be on the face of it a reason why exhibits which are marked for identification shouldn't be disclosed either, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I don't have argument why they shouldn't, Your Honour. I'm just not sure about logistically -- for example, I know Mr. Milosevic has tendered a number of items that have been marked for identification only, and I don't know how much of that we have received, whether we have full sets or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand the problem of the mechanics of this. I think the principle is probably that the material should be disclosed. It's a question of working out how to do it. So, again, I'll draw the issue to the attention of the Registrar because I think the ongoing material, the ongoing evidence that counsel here will be concerned about is largely defence evidence and largely defence exhibits, and I will leave it to counsel, the matter having been raised in the transcript, to sort it out with the Registrar. Now, the next motion also concerns Mr. Pavkovic, and that is a motion to set aside the joinder order or, in the alternative, to sever his case from that of the other five accused. Now, Mr. Ackerman, I need to be clear about the factual position in relation to this motion. You say that you were assigned on the 13th of June. The motion for joinder was not served upon counsel for the accused, nor was the new counsel - that's you - advised that such a motion was pending and needed to be answered within a stated period of time. Now, I noticed yesterday in the hearing that you attended in relation to the question of provisional release that there is reference in the Prosecution's response to this motion. Did that not alert you to the need to do something about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really don't recall there being a reference in that response, but I certainly take your word for it. If you say it was there, it was. The answer is no, it didn't alert me. I apparently overlooked it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to find the document myself. Yes, paragraph 5 of that response. On the 1st of April, the Prosecution filed a motion to join the case against General Pavkovic and his three co-accused with the case against the three accused of case number, and the case number is given. At the present time, that motion is pending before the Trial Chamber, and this was filed on the 24th of June, which is two months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can't argue that it's not there, Your Honour because it is there. I don't have any memory of seeing it. That's all I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where does that put your claim that you had weren't on notice about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me give just you a bit history about my assignment. I was assigned, as I said, on the 13th of June, and within -- I would say within two or three days, and I can give you the exact date because I still have the e-mail, I believe, I was advised by the Registry that the Chamber had asked the Registry to advise me that if I had any kind of a motion to file under Rule 72 with regard to the indictment the Chamber would like to receive it by the 1st of July, and so I was aware at that point the Chamber was advising me that there are matters that needed to be dealt with and that was one of them. The -- also, the order assigning me to the case asked the provisional counsel that had been assigned to provide me with any outstanding matters that needed to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, I think -- I accept from the information available to me that the motion wasn't formally served on the preceding counsel for your client, so even if she did pass on all the material it wouldn't have included this particular motion probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It may very well be, Your Honour, that I should have -- should have noticed what was in that response the Prosecution filed and made some inquiry but I can tell you that I did not, and that's the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it raises, I think, for the Chamber the question whether it's right to say that there was no notice to your client of the motion, and that is a important issue in deciding whether your application to set aside should be granted. There are two ways of dealing with this, I think. We could look at that application on its own on the purely technical basis of whether or not there was adequate notice given, or we could look at the whole picture in the light of any comments you wish to make about the merits of the motion for joinder. Now, in view of the general state of play here, the latter might be the better course. I'm inclined to the view that time is -- the time for the trial -- the trial is so far away anyway that it would be wrong to hold it against you, that perhaps you should have picked it up and made a response. If your inclination was to accept that the right thing to do now was to complete your response on the merits and let the Chamber look at your position on the basis that you've had an opportunity to state all that you want to state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, yeah, from a very intensely practical standpoint that's obviously the way to go. It wouldn't make sense to -- to order the filing of a new motion and give me an opportunity to response to that new motion and then make a new decision regarding the joinder. I think the motion that I filed to set aside the joinder could very well be taken as a -- as a document in opposition to the joinder because most of the reasons that I'd be opposed are contained in there in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying you don't really need time to amplify these, that the argument's there and the Chamber can proceed on the basis that you've not only dealt with the technicalities but the merits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The arguments that I have regarding the joinder, Your Honour, basically boil down to that -- that portion of the joinder decision in which the Chamber said we see no reason why this trial can't begin in December or January, and I have set out, I think, a number of reasons why in the interests of justice that can't happen, and I certainly would like to -- to speak further to that at an appropriate time, maybe when you get to that portion of your agenda regarding trial time or something like that, or if you'd like me to do it now I can do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think we'll take it in its place and treat what you say as a supplementary submission in support of the motion you've made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's probably the appropriate way to handle it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thanks very much. That's very accommodating of you, Mr. Ackerman, and it allows the Chamber, I think, to take a pragmatic course to a situation which basically is no one's fault but arises through a combination of circumstances which affect this particular accused and the way in which he came before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, in regard to that last matter. To the extent that we might have any right to reply to his supplement, we waive that right, and we're comfortable to Your Honour ruling on the motion based on the prior pleadings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Now, that leaves one motion, but I think probably the most important of the motions, and that's a motion to amend the indictment, which is accompanied with -- accompanied by an amended indictment reflecting the decision to conjoin the two cases. So I'd be assisted by some guidance on how you envisage this now being dealt with. Perhaps Mr. Hannis might suggest a course of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, was there -- I guess I'm not sure what your specific question is at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, your motion is to amend the indictment. That will have to be responded to in some way. How did you envisage that being done? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I envisaged the Court giving the Defence an opportunity to object and the Court considering that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The motion was filed on the 16th of August, so do you simply assume the normal two-week period for responding would apply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Hannis, I think the order that was originally made required or at least allowed 15 -- or allowed a response within 14 days, I think, from the -- 15 days from the 15th of August, and the filing was actually, for some minor technical reason, made on the 16th. So you would envisage that simply taking its ordinary course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, one problem that has been drawn to my attention is one of translation. What you've got is an indictment which is in English. What you've heard here today is that a number of the lead counsel are conducting the proceedings in the language of the accused. The accused themselves are entitled normally to see an indictment in a language that they can read, and I think I've been given an indication that translation might take until the middle of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what my case manager confirms to me, Your Honour. In fairness, it seems to me the defendants should have 15 days from the time that they actually receive a copy in their language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Even though there's -- on each team there's a person who can conduct the proceedings in English and even though the issues here are legal issues on which an accused might have some view but you wouldn't expect his input to be the most significant by any means?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. But I'm trying to imagine myself sitting on the other side the courtroom and what I would want. And it doesn't seem like it's the kind of thing where I can suggest to Your Honour to split the baby and give them seven and a half days. I just don't know what to recommend at this point. I wish we could have a translation quicker but it doesn't seem that we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who actually deals with that? Is it the Tribunal's translation service or is it the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: CLSS, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. O'Sullivan, what comments have you to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, you were, the position of the accused, I've spoken to all the counsel, and we would ask for 15 days from the time we receive the translated indictment in B/C/S. We see it as giving an opportunity for our clients to read and understand the indictment, and it's our submission that those 15 days wouldn't prejudice the accused or these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in spite of the view that I originally formed that that might not be necessary, it would be childish of me I think to ignore what has been said on the part of the Prosecution by Mr. Hannis, so I'm willing to make that order. So far as the content of any response is concerned, do you agree that a challenge to the indictment in its new form would be something which ought to be raised in the response to the motion to amend the indictment? Does Mr. Fila wish to say something or do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am prepared to accept your proposal. I personally believe that for the three of us who were here from the beginning, there will be no problems. We think it would be silly to repeat what was written concerning the first indictment. However, we have a double problem now. There are two new indictees who have not yet pled to the first indictment at all, so the legal position is different. It's different for the first three accused, Milutinovic, Sainovic, and Ojdanic in relation to the other three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may not --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I do not see any reason to object unless you want me to object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may not be aware of all that's gone on in relation to the other accused. Both Lazarevic and -- sorry? Yes indeed, but both Lazarevic and Lukic challenge the indictment, and the Chamber ruled on these challenges. Part of that ruling was that the Prosecution should review the indictment in relation to all six accused, and therefore -- and also in the case of Mr. Pavkovic a similar determination was made, although the real -- the crux of the matter was dealt with in the objections taken by -- on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Now, that means, I think, that all six are in the same position. The indictment is to be amended, according to Prosecution. I expect opposition to that amendment for reasons which I think were discussed at the 65 ter Conference, and there may be others, but it seems to me that if you are challenging the form of the indictment that the appropriate way to do it when an amendment is involved is to incorporate these challenges into your opposition to the motion to amend. It's a one-stage rather than two-stage process as I see it at the moment. Now, if anyone disagrees with that, then I'd like to hear their submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned that's fine. That's precisely what I meant, that we shouldn't make it a double burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it that silence on the part of everyone else confirms that that is how you intend to approach the matter. And that is helpful, because again with so many accused involved, we do not want to be bogged down -- it's in nobody's interest to be bogged down on technical arguments over things which we can resolve at a meeting such as this one. So the order which -- there will be written order following today's proceedings, and it will deal with the period -- extending the period for filing these -- or making these filings in opposition to the Prosecution motion. Now, Mr. Hannis, we seem to have more or less completed the disclosure of expert witness reports, and all that's outstanding is a translation of the latest report by Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and I understand we expect that in late September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can I take it by the 30th of June each of the last three accused had received disclosure of all the other expert reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I'm addressing myself to counsel for Pavkovic, Lazarevic, and Lukic. None of you has, as far as I'm aware, submitted any filing in relation to expert reports. That may be because of the weight of material that you're working your way through; I'm not sure. But in the case of each of the first three accused, there are various notices under Rule 94 bis in relation to each of the experts, and while they differ in form, the position of each of the accused is broadly similar in relation to each expert how they I tend to challenge that, that expert. It's not entirely similar, but through clarification as we've gone along they appear to be broadly taking the same line. Your time for actually submitting notices has expired except in relation to Mr. Coo, probably, because the translation is outstanding, and he may be the only one that matters for any of you; I don't know. But I draw this to your attention, because if you are going to raise peculiar points about expert evidence that have not been raised by the other three accused, it seems to me that should be done now or within the next -- I can indicate now I'm proposing quite an early either Status Conference or maybe a 65 ter Conference in this case. I don't think the next one will be in December. It will be much earlier. So if it's, say, in six weeks or so, then I would expect within that time-scale any challenge that you see as different from the way in which each of the counsel for the first three accused see the expert evidence would have been intimated, and I think you ought to take the opportunity of either aligning yourselves with the others or making it clear that you don't intend to challenge in a similar way. In other words, you should check the various filings that relate to the expert witnesses, check the expert reports and take a position within that time-scale. Now, the reason that I consider this important I explained the last time we had a Status Conference in relation to the first three accused, and I think I may also have expressed it to Mr. Bakrac before when he appeared, the Defence in this case have in my opinion a duty to try to coordinate their responses to expert evidence, and if there is to be Defence expert evidence, that unless an accused has an entirely distinctive position from the others, there would seem to be little reason why he cannot rely on the same expert as the other accused. That might require some internal wrangling among accused -- among counsel for the various accused, but it should be possible to identify common experts, and hopefully that can be done sometime within the next four or five months on the part of the Defence so that when the Prosecution case does begin at least the expert challenges are clear on the face of it. So I invite each of you for Messrs. Pavkovic, Lazarevic, and Lukic to look at the expert evidence so that we can see how identical your position will be to that of the other three accused. And again I think I would be inclined to make an order to that effect. Now, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my reaction to that is that based upon the overwhelming task that is ahead of us in preparing for this case, these expert reports are simply one small part of that huge body of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. material. What -- what you seem to be saying to us today is in the process of prioritising the way we go about that, you'd like us to begin there and deal with those expert matters first. I -- I don't know enough to tell you how much of a problem that is because -- because of the amount of material, but it may very well be that it's only a document that I'll be able to see months from now that will dictate the position I would have to take with regard to a particular expert. That may be the case. So if -- if you want a position taken within the period of time you've suggested, then it would simply have to be a seat of the pants kind of protect my client in every way possible, agree to nothing and demand cross-examination and just leave it at that and that may be the best I'd be able to do. I haven't even seen the expert reports yet. I know that they're -- they're at my office. I know that they're accessible to me, but I have no idea what's contained in them. I understand the Coo report is huge and would take a long time to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Four of these experts have been challenged on a broader basis than simply we want to cross-examine them and that's a view, I'm sure, you can form without being privy to the contents of all the disclosed material. You should be able to form a view about a person's expertise by considering his CV and his report. So there are certain things you can undoubtedly do. I note what you say. I hear what you're saying, but that's simply an indication that later you may have to alert the Court to a particular position that you weren't able to at the stage that you were expected to respond. But I remind you the Rule makes it clear, you have a certain time to respond to expert reports, I am reminding you of the terms of that Rule, time is already up, so I'm simply alerting you to the importance of concentrating some effort on that particular area and making the appropriate filings. And you may find that it's a lot easier than -- a much simpler task than you are currently envisaging.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I hope so. I can tell you right now that I understand this proposed expert Coo actually is an employee of the Office of the Prosecutor who was involved in investigating this case, and it's bizarre to me that such person could be termed an expert. He would never be an expert in my country or in your country as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's one of the -- that's one that I don't anticipate there will be very much agreement about, whereas the others I think -- or some of the others, not them all, some of the others fall into a different category, and I'm trying to concentrate efforts in areas that will eliminate unnecessary disputes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think you've clarified it for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And it's important that you're on notice of the significance of this. Mr. Scudder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCUDDER
utterances.text: Yes. I concur in the statements just made by Mr. Ackerman. And in addition, the Court mentioned that it urges counsel to agree as far as possible on these expert reports unless a particular defendant is in a different position than the other defendants, and I don't think because we haven't seen these reports yet I'm in a position to say anything definite at this time but I thought would I mention to the Court that Mr. Lukic has been a police official, and as I read the indictment most of the references are separately either to military or police. The only other police defendant in the case is Vlastimir Djordjevic, who is not before the Court, and that may put Mr. Lukic in a unique position regarding the experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may find it does in relation to one rather than the experts entirely. All right. I note what you say. Now, just one final point on experts. Is it Mr. Visnjic who was going to consider or had decided to challenge the qualifications of the witness Joachim? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are having a slight problem with the interpretation, but I believe that I know who you are talking about, but it seems to me that we have already challenged his qualification in the filing that we submitted. I don't know the exact date because I don't have the filing before me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: One matter about the experts, and that is the -- we did receive the Coo military report on the 31st of July, and we are still awaiting the B/C/S translation of that. And I would ask that your order for notices under Rule 94 bis reflect the fact that we would like to have a reasonable period after receiving the B/C/S translation of that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm in no doubt that your request in this case is justified, more so than in relation to the indictment, I may say. But, yes, you will be allowed adequate time after the translation. The indications are the end of September, so when you get it I think you can take it for granted that you've got 30 days from then to indicate any challenge or to respond in terms of 94 bis as you consider appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: One further matter in relation to witnesses, and I'm not sure whether you were about to deal with Rule 66, but it's correct that witness statements have been disclosed to the accused for some time in this case. However, at the 65 ter meeting two days ago, the Prosecution indicated that there would be further witnesses as and when they are identified and also further documents or potential exhibits as and when identified, and that the Prosecution is making its final determinations in light of evidence that's being led in the Milosevic case. So it appears that Rule 66 will be ongoing, that disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In light of the joinder, we believe that we probably will be adding witnesses to the number that we had previously indicated, that the trial will take somewhat longer than previously indicated for the original three defendants. And those numbers and the exhibits are going to be increased partly as a result of what has -- what has transpired in the Milosevic trial recently. A number of Defence witnesses called have produced I think a few hundred documents that we had not seen before that we think are pertinent to the prosecution of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But you're indicating now what, that there are witnesses to be thought about or you've identified them or what is the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Both, Your Honour. It's making a determination about -- in a joint case these three -- the three new accused we anticipate calling some witnesses that might not have been called in the original case because they deal more specifically with military or police matters than with the political matters. And because of some of the new information we have -- we have come to understand in light of interpretation of new evidence from the witnesses and documents in the Milosevic case causes us to think that we should call additional witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does any of -- does any of this plan to introduce other witnesses that relate to the concept that's been introduced into the case of indirect co-perpetratorship or joint control over the criminal conduct of forces or is it related to something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not necessarily, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've been struggling with this concept, I have to say, since it appeared and have been trying to understand what it's about. But that's not the source of the additional -- the need for additional witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. And it's a matter -- it's matter of quality of evidence and efficiency of preparation, Your Honour. One thing that's happening in course of ongoing analysis of information and contacting new potential witnesses as a result of some of those analyses sometimes we find ourselves in the position of having an insider witness, perhaps a Serb who was a soldier or policeman or -- on the inside, who may be able to testify not only about deportation but about a killing as well, and we make a decision about, well, do we call that witness to replace our current listed victim of a deportation or as a supplement to. It depends on a lot of circumstances. Did that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It concerns me that rather than becoming a bit simpler as the result of the review of the indictment the case seems to get increasingly more complex, and one can only have sympathy then for the Defence when the goal-posts are moving and material is not completely disclosed and accused have been before the Tribunal for more or less three years in some instances. It's depressing to find that that's the state of play, and it's very difficult to see that the plan that was in mind to get things going at the turn of the year can be fulfilled, in fact. THE PROSECUTOR: I understand, Your Honour. I share that depression. I can only tell you in the last trial I participated in we were talking about events that happened in 1992, and even up to the last month of trial we were finding out new information and bringing in new witnesses even at that point in time. However, it was our view that it was in the interest of justice and of assistance to the trier of fact to have the best information possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no doubt that that's the case, but what you expect is perhaps something to supplement the case that is already there. What we're seeing here is the case itself changing a little as you -- as you amend and that will inevitably, I think, cause some sort of delay in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. actually getting to trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. But that again also is partly a reaction and reflection to the change in and the changing jurisprudence in the Tribunal. What was written in the original indictment, you know, the law of joint criminal enterprise seems to be moving a little bit from where it was in 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. This may be the appropriate time to raise this because we're talking about changes to the playing field, as you've called it, and I'm sure Your Honour has seen in the joinder indictment there's also a very, very important addition to this indictment and that is the allegation that all seven accused in this indictment are responsible for alleged crimes which were committed in 1998. This is the first time that any allegations in a Kosovo indictment, of any of the previous Kosovo indictments allege liability of these accused for 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand the indictment period to be extended to 1998. What's being said is that knowledge of events and indeed participation in events in 1998 brings home a basis for inferring involvement in the joint criminal enterprise or for inferring knowledge and intent necessary to establish participation in the joint criminal enterprise. However, I see the point you're making in any event that it's necessary to prove the events in 1998 before you can then rely upon these as a basis for inferring the things that the Prosecution may seek to infer from these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think it's being suggested that you should be held criminally responsible and sentenced for these.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe there's -- I accept what Your Honour has said, but I believe it does go further in relation to Mr. Milutinovic. In paragraph 36(e) it says he promoted, instigated, facilitated, encouraged, and/or condoned the perpetration of crimes during 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are any of these specified?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, they're not, which may go to the form of the indictment. Or I can choose look at Mr. Lazarevic where it says -- paragraph 58(f) refers to the crimes charged in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I noticed the use -- I think it's only in relation to him, is it, that the word "charge" is actually used.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And also -- yes, it may have been in relation to General Pavkovic I picked up the use of the word "charged," but it may be in fact in relation to more than one accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The other dimension to this is that this greatly broadens the work that we must do in preparing this case. Now these allegations that crimes were committed by the Serbs against Albanians in Kosovo brings into play, in my submission, a review of the Limaj proceedings or the Haradinaj case because we can anticipate the Prosecution calling evidence to suggest that crimes were committed against -- or by Serb forces. Well, to prepare that properly we have to look and see what the events were in 1998, and the best example we have here in this Tribunal are the two cases indicting Kosovar Albanians. We're in the same situation as we have been in many other cases in this Tribunal; the Lasva valley, for example, where HVO was on one side and the Bosnian army is on the other. And those are related cases now. And those are things which must be reviewed, and for the first time now we are being put on notice that the Prosecution intends to proceed this way, and it's going to affect us. Even the three original accused now, we must revisit evidence, we must revisit Milosevic, we must look at the Albanian cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do your pension policies mature?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do your pension policies mature? I think the point that you're making is a point for your submissions in relation to the motion to amend the indictment. And I think that was already discussed, was it not, at the meeting that there are a number of issues which -- which clearly we would expect to see featuring in any such challenge. But I note that it's a supplementary point that if the indictment is amended that -- in the way you highlight that that will extend the time necessary to prepare, but that's an issue we can only address once we see the decision on amending the indictment. Mr. Hannis, the point's been made that the allegations of criminal activity are now expanded into 1998, but it's not immediately obvious that there are specific occasions identified in the indictment when these 1998 crimes are said to have been committed. Now, you have from I think paragraph 95 onwards reference to events in Kosovo in very broad terms. Is that what's meant by the 1998 crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to ask you to listen to Mr. Stamp speak on this issue regarding particular allegations in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Certainly. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Reference to paragraph 95 includes what is referred to in the indictment itself, the new amended indictment, but there are other matters, and may I just go on to describe the other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are they already referred to in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are those other matters already referred to in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The other matters have been dealt with in detail in a previous pre-trial brief. What the indictment proceeds to do is to clarify either a request of the Chambers, the reasons why it could be inferred the accused possessed knowledge or may be said to have participated in the joint criminal enterprise in respect to the crimes charged in the indictment, and those crimes are referred to from paragraph 72 forward of the indictment. There are no new charges. So we're not inviting the Court to consider charges against the accused alleged to have been committed in 1998. However, events in 1998 are part of the context in which the events or the charges that occurred later on in 1999 occurred and ought to be considered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But where you say that Mr. Lazarevic and Mr. Pavkovic are charged with crimes committed in 1998, is that a -- just a slip of the pen?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. The Prosecution does not intend to allege that they have actually been charged with offences in 1998, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when you say that the accused, and you heard the example given by Mr. O'Sullivan, were responsible for instigating conduct in 1998, do you intend to lead evidence of specific incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In a general sense evidence has to be led, Your Honour, of the context, the pre-existing context which led up to the circumstances in which the counts charged in this indictment were committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say that all you intend to rely upon in that regard has already been set out in a pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the pre-trial brief in respect to the first three accused. What I'm trying to convey to the Court is that the Prosecution does not raise as new counts or new charges events relating to 1998. They are merely contextual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan, can you identify from that the material you've already been told about in the pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I don't believe the pre-trial brief or any previous indictment makes these allegations in connection to 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we're not in a position to resolve that matter at this stage. The issue is one which you now have a little more information on to address it in your submissions in response to the motion to amend the indictment, and it gives you time at least to consider how much notice you've previously been given of this. Now, the last time we had a Status Conference in Milutinovic we had an issue over how interviews were to be conducted of proposed 92 bis witnesses. These were interviews that were require to be carried out in a delicate fashion. Have we made any progress on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We had decided to wait until the other Defence counsel were in the case and decide whether or not they might be willing to go along with Mr. O'Sullivan's proposal and then see if we could work something out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. O'Sullivan, I think it's for you to take this matter up with counsel for Pavkovic, Lazarevic, and Lukic. They're going to have plenty to do, so hopefully they would willingly accept your offer to deal with some of this on their behalf, especially since the nature of the evidence is such that it's difficult to imagine that your interests are other than consistent. Now, I think, Mr. Ackerman, I'll hear what else you have to say about the joinder at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. My remarks basically go to, as I've suggested, that portion of the joinder order that talks about seeing no obstacle to a rather early trial. And I just want to inform Your Honour of where I think we stand upon what I know today. Since being assigned to this case, I've received I believe 206 CDs. That number may be a little soft; it may be 208 or 204. And I understand there are more to come. Mr. Bakrac tells me he's received 280, which means I may have another 74 or something headed my way. I don't know the basis for that discrepancy at all. In the time I've been assigned, I have concentrated a significant portion of my time on just trying to figure out what is on each of those CDs. I've managed to get through 80 of them in the last 30 days or so, and that doesn't mean I'm looking at them for content particularly but to determine what they are and thereby know whether to assign them to another member of my staff. For instance, a number of them are either one-hour or two-hour broadcasts of news programmes from Belgrade television during the course of the war in Kosovo. I can't understand a thing that's on those, and so I have to send those off to my co-counsel in Belgrade to have him look at them and determine what they contain. That process, obviously, is going to take a significant additional time just to make the preliminary decision regarding those, and then extracting the content is another matter entirely. There is the electronic disclosure materials. When I first came on the case, I think there were two batches there, maybe three. It's now risen to five just in the short time that I've been there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any reason to think, though, that that is material which isn't on the CDs?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's definitely not on the CDs. That's why it's in EDS. The things that are on the CDs are simply things that apparently could not be put in the EDS system. All the videos couldn't go in the EDS system. So everything in EDS is totally different from -- there maybe duplications because there always are, but basically it's totally different. There are five batches there. The Prosecution cannot tell me how many pages of material are there. The estimates that I've heard range between 250.000 pages and 1 million pages. The Prosecution can't tell me how many -- what -- what number of pages in that material represent Rule 68 material. Your Honour might have seen in my -- in my joinder motion the math regarding this. We throw these numbers around in this Tribunal to the point where they have, I think, lost meaning in in terms of the number of pages of discovery. 250.000 pages of material is an overwhelming amount of material, Your Honour. If you put it in binders at 500 pages per binder, you've got 500 binders of material. It's 500, 500-page books. I told you reading at two minutes per page, a 40-hour week, it would take 208 weeks just to read it. Just to read it. So two counsel working on it couldn't even complete in a year and get through the material. And that's the EDS material. There is all of the material from the Milosevic trial. I'm advised by other counsel in the case that it will require at least six months to work through that material and properly deal with that. If we have to deal with the Limaj and Haradinaj material because of the 1998 issue having -- the possibility that that will arise, that adds another rather large layer. There are the 12 expert reports that you've suggested today that I need to make a rather priority and get those and read through those. I don't have any idea how many pages that is and how long it will take me. We've discussed today that Rule 66 disclosure is not yet complete and there's more material coming my way. We don't know how many additional witnesses. We don't know how many additional documents. There are I don't know how many witness statements that are disclosed in various ways that I will need to deal with. Once we deal with them, then we'll have to make decisions about what we want to do with regard to any investigation we might want to carry out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that the 206 CDs plus the EDS material is not witness statements? Witness statements are over and above that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think they're contained within that material. I don't know but I think they are. I think that's -- it's fair to assume that they are. There's this -- there's the issue of 92 bis witnesses. I know at some point Your Honour is going to expect me to deal with the issue of 92 bis witnesses, and I don't see how I can do that until I have gone through all the material because it may very well be the last document I look at it will be the document that would -- that impeach a proposed 92 bis witness. So until I'm familiar with the material, I don't know how I can give Your Honour a -- any kind of a position with regard to whether or not I could agree to a 92 -- proposed 92 bis witness. And it's not -- and the thing that is so important, Your Honour, to understand, it is not just reading through the material. If that were all that was involved, it would make the matter much easier. It is analysing that material, correlating that material, cross-referencing that material, getting that material into some form so that if -- if I need in the future something that I remember having read as I go through this I'll know how to find it, where it is. I'll have cross-reference it had in some way that I can use of it. The other thing that -- that complicates the matter is as we go through these documents it will become clear that there are a number of documents, a number witness statements, a number of -- a large number of material that -- that needs to be discussed with the accused, in consultation with the accused. That takes hours and hours and hours of time, just those consultations, and the efficiency with which you can do that as I mentioned to you in the hearing yesterday may depend a great deal upon whether the accused is here or in Belgrade. But suffice it to say, that's another major big problem that we're facing. I've suggested if you just take the EDS material, reading it two minutes per page, two counsel, two years -- one year, two counsel, one year just to get through that, I think it's a reasonable estimate, Your Honour, that in compliance with the Statute of this Tribunal that I cannot be ready to try this case before about the fall of 2007, and that's if we don't have a major problem arising out of this new 1998 material which I didn't consider when I filed my opposition to the motion for joinder. It would be -- it would be malpractice and a violation of my oath as a counsel and a violation of the -- of the ethical standards both in the bar to which I belong and the -- and this Tribunal to go to trial without having properly prepared. I couldn't possibly go to trial with not having read, for instance, every page of the Rule 68 material. The Prosecution provides that on the proposition that this is material which might be exculpatory of the accused. Well, I can't possibly not read that, be familiar with it and understand it and announce to you that I'm ready to go to trial because I can't be. It's a huge problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, you certainly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're going to have a break shortly because we have little time left on the tape, so can you give me some indication of timing here? We're not far from the end of the Status Conference but it's in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think my speech is virtually ended, Your Honour. I think I've gone through -- I've gone through my list basically, and I'm actually kind of summing up think point. So I think I could simply say that -- that based upon what I've suggested to you I feel that I -- I am assigned to Mr. Pavkovic, and my job is to provide him the highest level of assistance of which I'm capable. I can't do that if I don't understand what the Prosecution's case is. I can't do that -- we have rules that provide for discovery. We have rules that provide the Prosecution must turn over certain materials. It would be a mockery of those rules if I were permitted time to read that material. And so that's what I have to say about that. I think we need significant time to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Now, I have noted the various things that were said by the Prosecution about the likely length of the case and the various things said by the counsel for the various accused at the 65 ter meeting. Is there anything else that anyone wishes to raise this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not from me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Scudder?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCUDDER
utterances.text: Judge, could I just say that on behalf of the other defendants added with Mr. Ackerman's client we have exactly the same reaction. I've been doing this for 40 years. In my jurisdiction, the circuit court of Cook County, which I'm told is the largest court in the United States, I had an appeal of the largest civil bench trial up to that time and had to read 10.000 pages, which I thought was large. Then I joined the US government, and we had a nine-month political trial called the Chicago 7 trial. We had a 100.000 pages to read, and when I see what is involved in this case it's bigger than anything I have ever seen before and so I have the same reaction Mr. Ackerman does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scudder. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am in full agreement with what has been said by Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Scudder. I've been on the case for some two to three months or, rather, I came to the case two to three months before them because Mr. Lazarevic came to the Tribunal earlier, but I have to adjust the mere technical issue of opening the CDs and transferring them to the hard disk is a complex one. Mr. Ackerman mentioned the CDs, 280. I didn't really count them but just to give you an example, to transfer a file of 150 gigabytes, just doing that alone, is a major task, let alone analysing the material. Therefore I support everything that has been said by my colleagues and believe that needs to be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Well, I think it's appropriate to bring these proceedings to a conclusion. What I propose to do is on the next occasion to have a 65 ter Conference which I will attend, which means that we probably won't have a Status Conference until December, but we will probably have a 65 ter Conference in October. Now, the date of that will depend on how the Trial Chamber deals with the question of amendment and also the position in relation to Mr. Ackerman's motion for Mr. Pavkovic. So that date will be announced at an appropriate time. Meanwhile, I simply urge all counsel to make every endeavour to become familiar with as much of the material as possible on the basis that the plan is still to have a trial at the earliest possible date, and therefore your duty is to commit yourselves fully to becoming as prepared as you possibly can at the earliest possible date. That brings these proceedings to an end, and I adjourn the sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: at 4.44 p.m.
